procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 28, 1967 of the Allahabad High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 2195 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The original 16 accused were tried in the Court of Session, where 11 were acquitted. The High Court, on appeal, confirmed the convictions of the remaining accused with some modifications and reduced their sentences. One appellant, Gopi, was convicted under s. 326 and s. 148 of the Indian Penal Code. Others were convicted under s. 147.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (five in number) appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against their conviction and sentences. The appeal was limited to a pure point of law regarding the legality of a search and the right to resist it in private defense.

issue.issue_text: Whether a search conducted by a police officer outside the territorial limits of his own police station is illegal.

facts: A Sub-Inspector from Chhainsa police station sought to search the appellants' house, which was located in the jurisdiction of another police station (Dankaur), in connection with a stolen buffalo.
The Sub-Inspector conducted the search himself instead of asking the Dankaur police to do it.
His stated reason was his belief that the Dankaur police were "mixed up with the accused party" and would not act promptly.
law: The court analyzed Sections 165 and 166 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
Section 165 normally limits a police officer's power to search to the territorial limits of their own police station.

However, Section 166(3) provides an exception. It allows an officer to conduct a search in another jurisdiction if they have reason to believe that requiring the local police to do so would cause a delay, which could result in the concealment or destruction of evidence.
application: The Court found the Sub-Inspector's explanation for acting himself—that the local police were colluding with the accused—to be believable and a compelling reason.
It reasoned that in the case of stolen cattle, "time is of the essence," as the animal could be quickly removed or mixed with a larger herd, making recovery difficult.

The Court determined that if the officer believed the Dankaur police would "take their own time" due to their connection with the accused, this constituted a valid reason to fear a delay that would lead to the loss of evidence (the buffalo).
Therefore, the officer's actions were justified under the exception provided by Section 166(3), giving him "full jurisdiction" to carry out the search himself.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the search was illegal. It held that the search was legally justified under Section 166(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure because the officer had a compelling reason to believe that involving the local police would cause a delay, potentially leading to the loss of the evidence he was seeking.

issue.issue_text: Whether the appellants were justified in resisting the search party in the exercise of the right of private defence.

facts: A police party, led by Sub-Inspector Kesar Singh, went to the appellants' house at night to search for a stolen buffalo.
The Sub-Inspector informed the appellants, Gopi and Munshi, that they were a police party who had come to conduct a search.
In response, the appellants and others raised an alarm and violently attacked the police party, causing injuries.
The appellants claimed they resisted because they thought the raiding party were dacoits dressed in police uniforms and were therefore acting in self-defence.
law: Under Section 166(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, a police officer can conduct a search in the jurisdiction of another police station if there is reason to believe that evidence might be lost due to the delay of involving the local police.
Under Section 114 of the Evidence Act, there is a presumption that official acts have been regularly performed.
application: The Court first determined that the appellants' claim of mistaking the police for dacoits was factually incorrect. The evidence showed that the Sub-Inspector had clearly communicated to the appellants that it was a police party conducting a raid for the stolen buffalo. Therefore, the appellants knew the identity of the party they were attacking.

The Court then addressed the legality of the search itself. It found the search was justified under Section 166(3) because the Sub-Inspector had reason to believe the local police were colluding with the accused. In the case of stolen cattle, time is critical, and any delay could lead to the loss of evidence, justifying the Sub-Inspector's decision to act promptly and independently.

Regarding the argument that the Sub-Inspector failed to record his reasons for the search, the Court noted a lack of evidence on this point. Applying the presumption of regularity of official acts, the Court presumed the officer had followed the correct procedure.
Since the appellants knew it was a police party and the search was deemed legal and bona fide, there was no basis for a right of private defence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellants' claim of a right to private defence because the evidence established that they were explicitly informed that the raiding party was the police before they attacked. The Court also found the search to be legal and bona fide, thus removing any justification for the appellants' resistance.

issue.issue_text: Whether the failure of the police officer to record his reasons in writing for conducting the search, as required by sections 165 and 166, rendered the search illegal.

facts: The appellants argued that the search was illegal because the Sub-Inspector failed to record his reasons in writing before conducting it, as required by sections 165 and 166 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
law: The Court invoked the legal principle of the presumption of regularity of official acts (mentioned in the text as being under s. 114 of the Evidence Act, 1872).
application: The Court first noted that no questions were ever put to the Sub-Inspector during the proceedings to find out whether he had, in fact, recorded his reasons or not.
Due to this lack of evidence on the record, the Court could not make a finding that the officer had failed in his duty.

Instead, the Court applied the presumption that official acts are performed regularly and correctly. Based on this presumption, the Court assumed that the Sub-Inspector must have taken the required precaution of recording his reasons.
The Court concluded that it could not hold the alleged failure against the prosecution because there was no material evidence to support the appellants' claim.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, holding that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, it must be presumed that the police officer had properly recorded his reasons for the search, in line with the legal presumption that official acts are performed regularly.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a search conducted by a police officer outside the territorial limits of his own police station is illegal.
appellant_arguments: The search was illegal because it was conducted by a police officer outside his own territorial jurisdiction.
respondent_arguments: The search was legal under section 166(3) as the officer had reason to believe that involving the local police would cause a delay, which could result in the stolen cattle being lost or moved.
The officer had full jurisdiction to conduct the search himself to avoid delay, especially given the time-sensitive nature of recovering stolen cattle.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the appellants were justified in resisting the search party in the exercise of the right of private defence.
appellant_arguments: The appellants had the right to resist the search party in the exercise of their right of private defence.
The appellants believed the raiding party consisted of dacoits dressed in police uniforms, and they filed a police report to this effect.
respondent_arguments: The appellants were not justified in their attack because the sub-inspector had clearly informed them that it was a police party.
The appellants had no reason to attack the police party, either by mistaking them for dacoits or in any other form of self-defence.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the failure of the police officer to record his reasons in writing for conducting the search, as required by sections 165 and 166, rendered the search illegal.
appellant_arguments: The search was illegal because the police officer failed to record his reasons in writing as mandated by sections 165 and 166.
respondent_arguments: There is no evidence to prove the officer failed to record his reasons, as he was never questioned about it.
Given the principle of regularity of official acts, the court should presume that the officer did record his reasons.
The illegality cannot be held against the prosecution as there is no material on record to support the claim.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A police officer is legally authorized to conduct a search in the jurisdiction of another police station if the officer has reason to believe that a delay caused by requesting the local police to perform the search would lead to the concealment or destruction of evidence. In cases of stolen cattle, where time is of the essence due to the risk of the animal being moved and mixed with others, this constitutes a valid reason for such a belief.
obiter: In the absence of evidence to the contrary, it can be presumed that an official act, such as a police officer recording reasons for a search, was performed regularly.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The search conducted by the police officer outside his territorial jurisdiction was legal and bona fide under the exception provided in section 166(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The officer had reason to believe that involving the local police would cause a delay that could result in the loss of the stolen buffalo, which constituted the evidence. Consequently, the appellants, having been informed that it was a police party, had no right of private defence and were not justified in resisting the search.
legal_tests_applied: Section 166(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, which allows a police officer to conduct a search in another jurisdiction if he has reason to believe that delay occasioned by requiring the local officer to conduct the search would result in the evidence being concealed or destroyed.
The legal presumption of the regularity of official acts, which allows a court to presume that an official has performed their duties correctly unless there is evidence to the contrary.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the search was illegal because it was outside the officer's jurisdiction failed because the court found it was a valid exception under section 166(3), as the officer reasonably believed that delay would lead to the loss of the stolen buffalo, especially given his suspicion that the local police were 'mixed up with the accused'.

The claim of a right to private defence was rejected because the court found that the 'accused were informed by him that it was the police party which had come and they had no reason to attack the police party either as dacoits or in self-defence in any other form.'

The argument that the search was illegal for failure to record reasons in writing was dismissed because no evidence was presented to prove this failure, as 'no question appears to have been put to the sub-inspector to elicit from him whether the reasons were recorded or not.' In the absence of such evidence, the court applied the presumption of regularity of official acts.
why_respondent_won: The search was deemed legal because the court accepted that the officer 'had full jurisdiction in taking recourse to sub-s. (3) of s. 166 and to carry out the search himself' due to the time-sensitive nature of recovering stolen cattle and the risk of evidence being lost through delay.
The appellants' resistance was proven to be unjustified because the court accepted that the police had identified themselves, negating any claim of self-defence against supposed dacoits.

The procedural challenge regarding the failure to record reasons was overcome because the court, citing the principle of regularity of official acts, presumed the officer had recorded his reasons, stating, 'we cannot hold this against the prosecution, because there is no material on which we can proceed.'
policy_considerations: The court acknowledged the practical realities of police investigations, noting that in certain cases, such as recovering stolen cattle, 'time is of the essence, because once the animal is removed and mixed up with others, it is very difficult to spot it,' thus justifying immediate action to prevent the loss of evidence.
